deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the historical Section 1 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1853/54, published by Dedekind 1867). It continues the account of the vibrating-string controversy from the previous page. There is no new derivation; the mathematical content is as follows.

(a) Daniel Bernoulli's superposition (Mém. Berlin 1753). The string can vibrate (according to the theory) as
y(x,t) = Σ_n a_n sin(nπx/l) cos(nπα(t − β_n)/l).
Each term satisfies y_tt = α² y_xx and vanishes at x=0 and x=l. Bernoulli considered this the most general motion because it explained all observed modifications of the vibration (simultaneous overtones).

(b) Bernoulli's supporting argument. A massless stretched thread loaded with N finite point masses has motions that decompose into N simple (normal-mode) vibrations, each with one common period for all masses. In modern terms, the system M q'' = −K q has N eigenmodes.

(c) Euler's reply (Mém. Berlin 1753, p.196 ff.). Against d'Alembert, Euler holds that f in y = f(αt+x) − f(αt−x) may be completely arbitrary on (−l, l), with period 2l. Bernoulli's solution is general if and only if the series a_1 sin(πx/l) + a_2 sin(2πx/l) + … and ½b_0 + b_1 cos(πx/l) + … can represent an arbitrary curve.
- The step is implicit and mine: write f(z) = ½b_0 + Σ (a_n sin(nπz/l) + b_n cos(nπz/l)).
- Then f(αt+x) − f(αt−x) = Σ sin(nπx/l)[2a_n cos(nπαt/l) − 2b_n sin(nπαt/l)].
- This equals Σ A_n sin(nπx/l) cos(nπα(t − β_n)/l), with A_n cos(nπαβ_n/l) = 2a_n and A_n sin(nπαβ_n/l) = −2b_n.
- So Bernoulli's form equals the d'Alembert–Euler form exactly when f admits such a Fourier expansion.

(d) Riemann's diagnosis. Everyone then assumed that transformations valid for an analytic expression (finite or infinite) hold for all values, except in special cases. Hence it seemed impossible that an algebraic, or any analytically given non-periodic, curve could be represented by such a series, and Euler decided against Bernoulli.

(e) Lagrange (Misc. Taurinensia I, 1759, 'Recherches sur la nature et la propagation du son'). He treated a massless thread with an arbitrary number of equal masses at equal spacing. He solved the finite system with great analytic skill, then let the number of masses tend to infinity, recovering Euler's results. Riemann judges the passage from finite to infinite unsatisfactory, so d'Alembert (Opuscules mathématiques I) could still claim greatest generality for his own solution. The positions of all three remained divided.

The page ends mid-sentence, leading into the next page's summary of their views on arbitrary functions.
errors: In the draft the displayed formula appears to read sin(n2πx/l) cos{(2nπα/l)(t−β_n)} (consistent with the previous page's Taylor formula sin(n2πx/l)cos(n2παt/l)). With fixed ends at 0 and l and f of period 2l, the correct modes are sin(nπx/l) cos(nπα(t−β_n)/l). The factor 2 would omit the odd harmonics, including the fundamental. The published 1867 text has nπ. If the 2 is really in the draft, it is a slip.

Historical nuance, not a mathematical error: the claim that Lagrange's limiting passage 'left much to be desired' is Riemann's (standard) judgment. Lagrange did in effect obtain Fourier-like integral formulas but did not draw the conclusion, as Riemann discusses on the following pages.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the well-known historical introduction of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. The content is an exposition of 18th-century results, essentially matching the printed text.

checkable.asserts: Each Bernoulli mode solves the wave equation y_tt = α² y_xx
Sine part of f yields a standing mode under y = f(αt+x) − f(αt−x)
Cosine part of f also yields a standing mode; the constant ½b_0 cancels, so the Euler/d'Alembert form with Fourier-expandable f equals Bernoulli's form
Massless string with 2 equal equally spaced masses has 2 normal modes (Bernoulli/Lagrange). Frequencies are ∝ sqrt(eigenvalues) = 2 sin(kπ/6), k=1,2
The modes sin(nπx/l) vanish at both fixed ends, including odd n (relevant to the 2π vs π slip)

transcription_corrections: First line: the manuscript reads '(der Theorie nach) auch nach der Gleichung' (cf. the published text), not '(der Saite auch nach der Gleichung'.
Displayed formula: the image appears to show a factor 2 (sin(n2πx/l), cos{(2nπα/l)(t−β_n)}), whereas the transcription gives nπ. The published version has nπ.
'Opuscules': the word 'analytiques' is struck through and replaced by 'mathématiques' above the line, as transcribed.
